findings.trigger_condition: The edge stream contains two equal values where one is hashable and the other is not (stdlib example: frozenset({1}) vs {1}, since frozenset({1}) == {1}), or user objects whose __hash__ is identity-based while __eq__ is value-based. E.g. dependency_layers([(2, frozenset({1})), (2, {1})]).
findings.root_cause: _id_of partitions the node registry by hashability: hashable values go into hash_buckets and are only compared against other hashable values in the same hash bucket, while unhashable values are only compared against the separate unhashable_ids/unhashable_nodes lists. An equal value that lands on the other side of the boundary is never seen as a duplicate, so it receives a fresh id. This contradicts the function's own docstring ('assigns each unique node value a monotonically increasing int id') and the dedup semantics of the contract. Because only one comparison direction is used (stored == value / candidate == value), the result also depends on which value was seen first.
findings.impact: The same logical node value appears multiple times in the output layers, breaking 'list[list[object]] with nodes deduplicated by value' and 'deduplicate repeated edges'. Verified: dependency_layers([(2, frozenset({1})), (2, {1})]) returns [[frozenset({1}), {1}], [2]] -- two distinct entries for one value and two edges where the contract sees one. Node count is inflated, layer contents are wrong, and indegree/blocked bookkeeping operates on duplicated identities. With hash-inconsistent user types (identity __hash__, value __eq__), equal nodes land in different hash buckets and the id replication can even mask a real directed cycle, so DependencyCycleError is not raised for input that logically contains a 2-cycle.
findings.suggested_validation: Feed a graph mixing hashable and unhashable equal nodes: assert frozenset({1}) and {1} collapse to a single node (e.g. expect [[{1}], [2]] for edges [(2, frozenset({1})), (2, {1})] and same result when the roles are reversed). Also construct a custom class with identity __hash__ and value __eq__ and verify equal-but-distinct instances used in a cycle ([(x1,y),(y,x2)] with x1==x2, x1 is not x2) raise DependencyCycleError; a value-based implementation must, this one may not.

findings.trigger_condition: The edge stream contains many distinct unhashable node values (lists, dicts, sets used as nodes). Measured: 5000 distinct list nodes -> 0.57s, 10000 -> 2.25s (4x runtime for 2x input, i.e. quadratic).
findings.root_cause: Dedup for unhashable values is a linear scan over all previously seen unhashable nodes (zip(unhashable_ids, unhashable_nodes) with an == comparison per pair), run inside _id_of on every edge endpoint. With U distinct unhashable nodes and E edges this is O(E*U) comparisons, and each == on a large list/dict is itself a deep comparison. The docstring even acknowledges the 'small list' assumption, but nothing bounds it.
findings.impact: Quadratic blowup on inputs with many unhashable nodes; at 50k distinct list nodes the dedup alone extrapolates to roughly a minute, and with large containers the deep-equality cost multiplies it further. The rest of the algorithm is O(V+E), so this path is the scaling bottleneck for exactly the 'arbitrary object node' inputs the contract's list[list[object]] signature invites.
findings.suggested_validation: Stress test with N distinct unhashable nodes (e.g. [[i] for i in range(20000)]) and assert runtime scales near-linearly or at least completes in a bounded time; alternatively inspect that dedup avoids rescanning all previous unhashables (canonicalize to a hashable form such as frozenset/nested tuples, or bucket by a structural fingerprint).

findings.trigger_condition: Node values whose __eq__ is asymmetric (value == candidate is True but candidate == value is False), or whose __hash__ raises TypeError for a reason other than being unhashable.
findings.root_cause: Both dedup paths evaluate equality in only one direction (stored == value / candidate == value), never value == stored, so a value that compares equal only from its own side is missed and registered as a new node. Additionally, the bare except TypeError around hash_buckets.setdefault treats any TypeError raised while hashing as 'unhashable', so a custom __hash__ that deliberately raises TypeError for its own purposes is silently reclassified to the unhashable path.
findings.impact: Deduplication silently fails for asymmetric equality, returning duplicate entries for one logical node; the TypeError misclassification is benign in most cases but means a hashable value is deduplicated by linear scan against the wrong registry, which can also duplicate nodes. Both are edge cases, but they compound the same 'one logical value, multiple ids' failure mode as F1.
findings.suggested_validation: Unit test with a class implementing __eq__ returning True only when self is on the left (__eq__ that compares self.__class__ to the operand) and __hash__ raising TypeError; verify each equal value maps to exactly one node regardless of encounter order.
